title: Drances et Turnus. Altercatio
titleEn: The Quarrel of Drances and Turnus — Aeneid XI.336–444
part: The Quarrel of Drances and Turnus (XI.336–444)
about: Latinus has proposed peace with the Trojans, and the first to rise in his council is Drances, an old enemy of Turnus: rich, eloquent, influential in faction, of noble birth on his mother's side, and no fighter. He backs the king's offer and asks him to add one more gift, his daughter Lavinia as bride for Aeneas, and then turns on Turnus by name. Turnus's ill-starred leadership, he says, has cost the Latins their best captains and filled the city with mourning; there is no safety in war; let Turnus give up his claim and go, or, if he wants the princess and the palace so badly, let him face Aeneas alone, for Aeneas is calling him out. Turnus blazes up. Drances, he answers, is always bold in words while the walls keep the enemy away; let him show his valour in the field, where the Trojans are near enough. Turnus recalls his own deeds, Pallas and the Arcadians killed, Pandarus and Bitias cut down inside the Trojan camp, and mocks Drances' terror of a twice-defeated people. Then he turns to Latinus: if all hope is gone, let them beg for peace; but the Latins still have men, allies, Messapus, Tolumnius, Camilla and her horsemen, and fortune has often turned. And if Aeneas wants him alone, Turnus will meet him, even if he proves a second Achilles in armour made by Vulcan; he has devoted his life to his people and his king. The debate is Virgil's version of a Roman senate-house quarrel, and Drances, the clever civilian who goads a soldier, echoes Homer's Thersites and Polydamas while being neither.

sentences.t:
Tum Drances idem infensus, quem gloria Turni
obliqua invidia stimulisque agitabat amaris,
largus opum et lingua melior, sed frigida bello
dextera, consiliis habitus non futilis auctor,
sentences.l:
Then Drances, the same hostile one, whom the glory of Turnus
with sidelong envy and with goads was driving, bitter ones,
lavish of wealth and in tongue better, but cold for war
his right hand, in counsels held a not futile adviser,
sentences.i: Then Drances, hostile as ever, a man whom the glory of Turnus spurred on with the bitter goads of a jealous, sidelong envy; lavish with his wealth and better with his tongue, though his sword-hand was cold in war, he was held to be no worthless counsellor,
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'idem infensus', 'the same man, hostile', the Drances who spoke against Turnus at the truce (122–131). 'obliqua invidia', 'with envy looking askance'; 'stimulis… amaris', 'with bitter goads', framing the verb. 'largus opum', 'generous of wealth', genitive with an adjective; 'lingua melior', 'better in tongue', ablative of respect. 'frigida bello dextera', the right hand that should strike is 'cold' in war. 'habitus', 'considered'; 'consiliis', dative or ablative, 'in debate'. The main verb waits until 342 ('surgit'). Elisions 'ide(m) infensus', 'obliqu(a) invidia', 'stimulisqu(e) agitabat', 'op(um) et'.

sentences.t:
seditione potens (genus huic materna superbum
nobilitas dabat, incertum de patre ferebat),
surgit et his onerat dictis atque aggerat iras:
sentences.l:
in sedition powerful (birth to him from his mother proud
nobility gave, uncertain from his father he bore),
rises, and with these loads, words, and heaps up angers:
sentences.i: powerful in faction (his mother's high rank gave him proud descent; his father's he brought with him uncertain), he rose, and with these words loaded and heaped up the anger:
sentences.n: 'seditione potens', 'powerful in civil strife', able to sway a crowd, a Roman type. The parenthesis gives his birth: 'genus… superbum… nobilitas dabat', 'nobility on the mother's side gave him proud birth'; 'incertum de patre ferebat', 'from his father he carried (a birth) uncertain', the noun 'genus' understood: his father was obscure, or unknown; the words allow either. 'onerat… aggerat iras', 'loads and piles up the angers', the metaphor of building a rampart (agger) of hatred against Turnus. 'surgit', vivid present, as speakers rose in the Roman senate. Elision 'atqu(e) aggerat'.

sentences.t:
“Rem nulli obscuram nostrae nec vocis egentem
consulis, O bone rex: cuncti se scire fatentur,
quid fortuna ferat populi, sed dicere mussant.
sentences.l:
“A matter to no one obscure and not of our voice needing
you consult on, O good king: all themselves to know confess
what the fortune of the people brings, but to say it they hesitate, muttering.
sentences.i: “You ask our counsel, good king, on a matter that is dark to no one and has no need of any word from us: all confess they know what the fortune of the people portends, but they only mutter and dare not say it.
sentences.n: Drances' speech begins. 'Rem… consulis', 'you consult (us) on a matter', 'consulo' with the accusative of the thing asked about. 'nulli obscuram', 'unclear to nobody'; 'nostrae… vocis egentem', 'needing our voice', 'egeo' with the genitive. 'O bone rex', a respectful vocative. 'quid fortuna ferat populi', indirect question, 'what the fortune of the people brings': ruin, if the war goes on. 'mussant', 'they mutter, hesitate to speak', from fear of Turnus; Drances casts himself as the one brave enough to speak out. Elision 'null(i) obscuram'.

sentences.t:
Det libertatem fandi flatusque remittat
cuius ob auspicium infaustum moresque sinistros
(dicam equidem, licet arma mihi mortemque minetur)
lumina tot cecidisse ducum totamque videmus
consedisse urbem luctu,
sentences.l:
Let him give freedom of speaking and the blusterings let him remit,
on account of whose auspices ill-omened and character perverse
(I will say it indeed, though arms to me and death he threaten)
the lights so many to have fallen of leaders and the whole we see
to have sunk the city in grief,
sentences.i: Let him grant us freedom to speak and abate his blustering pride, the man under whose ill-starred leadership and perverse ways (yes, I will say it, though he threaten me with arms and death) we see so many of our leaders, the lights of our people, fallen, and the whole city sunk in grief,
sentences.n: Turnus is not named: 'Det… remittat', jussive subjunctives, 'let him give… let him abate', with the antecedent of 'cuius' left as 'he'. 'flatus', 'blasts, puffs', of his arrogance. 'ob auspicium infaustum', 'because of his unlucky auspices': a Roman general fought under his own auspices, so defeat was his. 'mores… sinistros', 'perverse character', 'sinister', 'left', the unlucky side. 'lumina… ducum', 'the lights of leaders', a bold metaphor. 'cecidisse… consedisse', accusative and infinitive after 'videmus'. Elisions 'auspici(um) infaustum', 'dic(am) equidem', 'consediss(e) urbem'.

sentences.t:
dum Troia temptat
castra fugae fidens et caelum territat armis.
sentences.l:
while the Trojan he assails
camp, in flight trusting, and heaven he terrifies with arms.
sentences.i: while he makes his attempt on the Trojan camp, trusting to flight, and frightens heaven with the clash of arms.
sentences.n: 'dum… temptat', 'while he assails', the present with 'dum'. 'Troia… castra', the Trojan camp, the adjective and noun across the line-break. 'fugae fidens', 'trusting in flight', a sneer, perhaps glancing at his escape from inside the camp by a leap into the Tiber (IX.815–818). 'caelum territat armis', 'he frightens the sky with arms', all noise and no result; the frequentative 'territat' adds to the scorn. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Unum etiam donis istis, quae plurima mitti
Dardanidis dicique iubes, unum, optime regum,
adicias nec te ullius violentia vincat,
quin natam egregio genero dignisque hymenaeis
des, pater, et pacem hanc aeterno foedere iungas.
sentences.l:
One thing also to those gifts, which very many to be sent
to the Dardanians and to be promised you order, one thing, best of kings,
may you add, and not you anyone's violence conquer,
but that your daughter to an outstanding son-in-law and worthy marriage
you give, father, and this peace with an eternal treaty bind.
sentences.i: To those gifts, so many, that you order to be sent and promised to the Dardanians, add one thing more, best of kings, one thing, and let no man's violence overcome you: give your daughter, father, to a son-in-law of distinction in a worthy marriage, and bind this peace with an everlasting treaty.
sentences.n: 'Unum… unum', the repetition holds back what the gift is. 'donis istis', dative with 'adicias', 'add to those gifts', the ones Latinus proposed (333–334). 'adicias', jussive subjunctive, a polite command; its first syllable is long, as if 'adiicias'. 'nec te ullius violentia vincat', 'and let not anyone's violence defeat you', meaning Turnus's. 'quin… des… iungas', 'from giving… and binding', 'quin' after the idea of prevention. 'egregio genero', Aeneas, unnamed. 'hymenaeis', Greek, 'marriage', a four-syllable line-end. Elisions 'Un(um) etiam', 'un(um) optime', 't(e) ullius', 'nat(am) egregio', 'dignisqu(e) hymenaeis', 'pac(em) hanc'.

sentences.t:
Quod si tantus habet mentes et pectora terror,
ipsum obtestemur veniamque oremus ab ipso:
cedat, ius proprium regi patriaeque remittat.
sentences.l:
But if so great holds minds and breasts terror,
himself let us beseech, and favour let us beg from himself:
let him yield, his own right to the king and country let him give up.
sentences.i: But if such terror holds our minds and hearts, let us beseech the man himself and beg the favour of him in person: let him give way and surrender his own claim to the king and to his country.
sentences.n: 'Quod si', 'but if'. 'tantus… terror', framing the line. 'ipsum… ab ipso', 'the man himself… from the man himself', heavy irony: if Turnus is so feared, the council must plead with him as with a lord. 'obtestemur… oremus', hortatory subjunctives, 'let us beseech… let us beg'. 'cedat… remittat', jussive, 'let him yield… give back'. 'ius proprium', 'his own right', his claim to Lavinia's hand, which only he can surrender. Elisions 'ips(um) obtestemur', 'veniamqu(e) oremus'.

sentences.t:
Quid miseros totiens in aperta pericula cives
proicis, O Latio caput horum et causa malorum?
sentences.l:
Why the wretched so often into open dangers citizens
do you throw forward, O for Latium the head and cause of these evils?
sentences.i: Why do you fling our unhappy citizens so often into open danger, you, the source and cause of all these evils for Latium?
sentences.n: Now Drances turns and speaks to Turnus directly, an abrupt address (apostrophe). 'miseros… cives', framing the line. 'in aperta pericula', 'into dangers in the open', 'proicis', 'you throw forth', as if they were things to be thrown away. 'caput… et causa', 'head and cause', the alliteration sharpening the charge; 'caput', 'fountain-head, origin'. 'Latio', dative of disadvantage. Elision 'hor(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Nulla salus bello: pacem te poscimus omnes,
Turne, simul pacis solum inviolabile pignus.
sentences.l:
No safety in war: peace you we ask, all,
Turnus, and at the same time peace's sole inviolable pledge.
sentences.i: There is no safety in war: we all ask you for peace, Turnus, and with it the one pledge that can keep a peace unbroken.
sentences.n: 'Nulla salus bello', 'no safety in war', a short, quotable verdict; Turnus will throw these exact words back at 399. 'pacem te poscimus', 'posco' with two accusatives, the thing and the person asked. 'Turne', vocative, held to the start of the next line. 'pacis… inviolabile pignus', 'the inviolable pledge of peace', Lavinia, whose marriage to Aeneas would bind the treaty; she is not named. Elision 'solu(m) inviolabile'.

sentences.t:
Primus ego, invisum quem tu tibi fingis, et esse
nil moror, en supplex venio.
sentences.l:
First I, hateful whom you to yourself imagine, and to be so
I do not care, see, a suppliant I come.
sentences.i: I am the first, I whom you picture as your enemy (and I do not mind if I am), see, I come to you as a suppliant.
sentences.n: 'Primus ego', 'I first', taking the lead. 'invisum quem tu tibi fingis', 'whom you imagine (as) hateful to you'. 'et esse nil moror', 'and I care nothing about being so', 'moror' here 'pay heed to', with an infinitive. 'en', 'look', drawing attention to the gesture. 'supplex', the suppliant's humility is false and the insult is real. Elision 'eg(o) invisum'.

sentences.t:
Miserere tuorum,
pone animos et pulsus abi.
sentences.l:
Pity your own,
put away your proud spirits and, beaten, go.
sentences.i: Take pity on your own people, lay aside your pride, admit you are beaten, and go.
sentences.n: 'Miserere', imperative of the deponent 'misereor', with the genitive 'tuorum', 'your people'. 'pone animos', 'put down your spirits', the plural 'animi' meaning pride, arrogance. 'pulsus abi', 'go, beaten', the participle doing the work of a clause: admit defeat and leave. Turnus will pick up 'pulsus' with fury at 392. Elision 'pon(e) animos'.

sentences.t:
Sat funera fusi
vidimus ingentis et desolavimus agros.
sentences.l:
Enough funerals, routed,
we have seen, and huge we have laid waste the fields.
sentences.i: We have been routed and seen enough deaths, and laid waste wide lands.
sentences.n: 'Sat', short for 'satis', 'enough', standing as an indeclinable adjective with 'funera'. 'funera', 'deaths, funerals'. 'fusi', 'routed', nominative plural agreeing with the 'we' of 'vidimus'. 'ingentis… agros', 'huge fields', '-is' accusative plural, the adjective set before 'et': the word order is 'et ingentis desolavimus agros'. 'desolavimus', 'we have emptied', by the war. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Aut si fama movet, si tantum pectore robur
concipis et si adeo dotalis regia cordi est,
aude atque adversum fidens fer pectus in hostem.
sentences.l:
Or if fame moves you, if so much in your breast strength
you conceive, and if so much a dowry palace to heart is,
dare and, facing, trusting, carry your breast against the enemy.
sentences.i: Or if glory stirs you, if you feel such strength in your heart, if a palace that comes as a dowry is so dear to you, then be bold, and bear your breast confidently to face the enemy.
sentences.n: Three conditions, 'si… si… si', each sharper than the last. 'fama', 'reputation, glory'. 'concipis', 'you conceive', as if strength were a passion. 'dotalis regia', 'a palace for a dowry', Latinus's kingdom coming with Lavinia; Drances says Turnus wants the throne, not the girl. 'cordi est', 'is to the heart', 'is dear', the predicative dative. 'aude', 'dare'; 'adversum' goes with 'pectus', 'your breast turned to face him', or with 'hostem', 'the enemy opposite'. Elisions 's(i) adeo', 'cord(i) est', 'aud(e) atque', 'atqu(e) adversum'.

sentences.t:
Scilicet ut Turno contingat regia coniunx,
nos animae viles, inhumata infletaque turba,
sternamur campis.
sentences.l:
No doubt so that to Turnus may fall a royal wife,
we, souls cheap, an unburied and unwept crowd,
must be strewn on the plains.
sentences.i: No doubt, so that Turnus may win a royal bride, we, lives of no account, a crowd unburied and unwept, must be strewn across the plains.
sentences.n: 'Scilicet', 'of course', bitterly ironic, as often. 'ut… contingat', purpose clause, 'so that (a royal wife) may fall to Turnus'. 'nos… sternamur', 'we are to be laid low', a jussive or indignant subjunctive. 'animae viles', 'cheap souls'. 'inhumata infletaque', 'unburied and unwept', the worst fate in the ancient world: the unburied could not cross the Styx (VI.325–330). The Latins have just been burying their dead under truce (203–212). Elision 'inhumat(a) infletaque'.

sentences.t:
Etiam tu, siqua tibi vis,
si patrii quid Martis habes, illum aspice contra,
qui vocat.”
sentences.i: You too, if there is any strength in you, if you have anything of your father's war-like spirit, look him in the face — the man who calls you out.”
sentences.n: 'siqua tibi vis', 'if (you have) any strength', 'siqua' printed as one word ('si qua'), 'tibi' dative of possession. 'patrii quid Martis', 'anything of your father's Mars', partitive genitive: Mars for warlike spirit, 'patrii', as Turnus's father Daunus was a fighter. 'illum… qui vocat', Aeneas, who said Turnus should have fought it out with him alone (115–118). 'contra', adverb, 'face to face'. 'qui vocat.' is one of Virgil's unfinished half-lines; the speech ends with it, abruptly. Elision 'ill(um) aspice'.

sentences.t: Talibus exarsit dictis violentia Turni;
sentences.l: At such words blazed up the violence of Turnus;
sentences.i: At such words Turnus's fierce temper flared;
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'exarsit', 'flared up', the image of fire, the regular word for sudden anger. 'violentia Turni', 'the violence of Turnus', the abstract noun as subject, picking up Drances' 'ullius violentia' (354): the speech provokes the very thing it complained of. 'violentia' is Turnus's word through the last books (XII.9, 45). No elisions.

sentences.t:
dat gemitum rumpitque has imo pectore voces
“Larga quidem, Drance, semper tibi copia fandi
tum, cum bella manus poscunt, patribusque vocatis
primus ades.
sentences.l:
he gives a groan and breaks out these from the bottom of his breast words:
“Abundant indeed, Drances, always to you the supply of speaking
then, when wars hands demand; and when the fathers are called,
first you are present.
sentences.i: he groaned, and these words burst from the depths of his breast: “You always have a full flow of words indeed, Drances, just when war calls for hands; and when the elders are summoned, you are the first to arrive.
sentences.n: 'dat gemitum', 'gives a groan'. 'rumpit… voces', 'bursts out words', as if the words broke through. Turnus's speech begins. 'Larga… copia fandi', 'an abundant supply of speaking', 'fandi' the gerund. 'Drance', Greek vocative. 'tum, cum…', 'just when', the irony in the timing. 'patribus vocatis', ablative absolute, 'the fathers (elders) having been summoned', Roman senators. The Latin Library places 'semper' before 'Drance'; the sense is unchanged. Elision 'rumpitqu(e) has'.

sentences.t:
Sed non replenda est curia verbis,
quae tuto tibi magna volant, dum distinet hostem
agger murorum nec inundant sanguine fossae.
sentences.l:
But not to be filled is the senate-house with words,
which safely to you big fly, while keeps apart the enemy
the rampart of walls and do not overflow with blood the ditches.
sentences.i: But the council-chamber is not to be filled with words, words that fly big and safe from your mouth while the rampart of the walls holds back the enemy and the trenches are not yet brimming with blood.
sentences.n: 'non replenda est', 'is not to be filled', the gerundive of obligation. 'curia', the Roman senate-house, a deliberate anachronism. 'quae… volant', 'which fly', words as winged things (Homer's 'winged words'). 'tuto', adverb, 'in safety'; 'magna', 'big', boastful. 'dum distinet hostem agger', 'while the rampart keeps off the enemy'; 'nec inundant… fossae', 'and the ditches are not flooding', 'dum' governing both. Elision 'replend(a) est'.

sentences.t:
Proinde tona eloquio, solitum tibi, meque timoris
argue tu, Drance, quando tot stragis acervos
Teucrorum tua dextra dedit passimque tropaeis
insignis agros.
sentences.l:
So thunder in eloquence, your habit, and me of fear
accuse, you, Drances, since so many of slaughter heaps
of Teucrians your right hand has made and everywhere with trophies
you mark the fields.
sentences.i: So go on, thunder with your eloquence, as you always do, and accuse me of cowardice, you, Drances, since your right hand has made such heaps of slaughtered Trojans, and you set up trophies all over the fields.
sentences.n: Bitter irony throughout. 'Proinde', 'so then', two syllables by synizesis. 'tona', 'thunder', of a loud orator. 'solitum tibi', 'a thing usual to you', in apposition to the whole command. 'timoris argue', 'accuse of fear', the genitive of the charge, a legal idiom. 'tot stragis acervos', 'so many heaps of slaughter'. 'insignis', second person singular of 'insignio', 'you mark, make conspicuous', not the adjective. 'tropaeis', trophies were enemy armour hung on a stake, as Aeneas did at the start of the book (XI.5–11). Elision 'ton(a) eloquio'.

sentences.t:
Possit quid vivida virtus,
experiare licet; nec longe scilicet hostes
quaerendi nobis: circumstant undique muros.
sentences.l:
What may achieve lively valour,
you may test; and not far, of course, the enemy
are to be sought by us: they stand around on every side the walls.
sentences.i: What living valour can achieve, you are free to find out; and certainly we need not go far to look for the enemy: they are all round our walls.
sentences.n: 'Possit quid vivida virtus', an indirect question, 'what lively valour can do', the object of 'experiare'. 'experiare licet', 'you may test', 'licet' with the subjunctive, 'experiare' an alternative form of 'experiaris'. 'scilicet', 'obviously', here dry rather than bitter. 'quaerendi nobis', 'must be sought by us', the gerundive with dative of agent. 'circumstant… muros', the Trojans are camped close by. No elisions.

sentences.t: Imus in adversos: quid cessas?
sentences.l: We go against the facing: why do you hang back?
sentences.i: Let us go out against them: why do you hang back?
sentences.n: 'Imus', 'we are going', the present used for an immediate future, almost 'let us go'. 'in adversos', 'against those facing (us)', the enemy, the adjective standing as a noun. 'quid cessas?', 'why do you delay?', to Drances, who has not moved. The short clauses imitate a man already on his feet. No elisions.

sentences.t:
An tibi Mavors
ventosa in lingua pedibusque fugacibus istis
semper erit?
sentences.l:
Or to you will Mars in a windy
tongue and in those runaway feet of yours
always be?
sentences.i: Or will your warfare always be in that windy tongue of yours and those feet so quick to run?
sentences.n: 'An', introducing a second, scornful question. 'Mavors', an archaic and poetic form of 'Mars', the god for war-making itself. 'tibi', dative of possession, 'will your Mars be'. 'ventosa in lingua', 'in a windy tongue', all air. 'pedibus… fugacibus istis', 'in those runaway feet of yours', 'iste' contemptuous, 'that… of yours'. 'semper erit?' is one of Virgil's unfinished half-lines, here falling, as at 375, at a sharp break in the speech. Elision 'ventos(a) in'.

sentences.t: Pulsus ego?
sentences.l: Beaten, I?
sentences.i: Beaten, am I?
sentences.n: Turnus seizes on Drances' word 'pulsus abi' (366), 'go, beaten', and throws it back as a question with no verb, 'beaten, I?', the indignation in the bare words. The next unit asks whether anyone could fairly call him so. No elisions within these words; 'ego' elides into 'Aut', across the question mark.

sentences.t:
Aut quisquam merito, foedissime, pulsum
arguet, Iliaco tumidum qui crescere Thybrim
sanguine et Evandri totam cum stirpe videbit
procubuisse domum atque exutos Arcadas armis?
sentences.l:
Or anyone justly, most foul one, beaten
will accuse, who swollen to grow with Ilian the Tiber
blood, and of Evander the whole with the stock will see
to have fallen the house and stripped the Arcadians of arms?
sentences.i: Or will anyone, you foulest of men, have the right to call me beaten, when he sees the Tiber rising swollen with Trojan blood, and the whole house of Evander fallen with all its line, and the Arcadians stripped of their arms?
sentences.n: 'merito', 'deservedly', 'justly'. 'foedissime', 'most foul', vocative to Drances. 'pulsum arguet', 'will charge (me as) beaten'. 'qui… videbit', 'who will see', with three accusative and infinitive clauses: the Tiber growing swollen with Trojan blood ('Iliaco… sanguine' framing), Evander's house fallen 'with its stock', since Turnus killed Pallas, his only son (X.479–489), and the Arcadians 'stripped of their arms'. 'Arcadas', Greek accusative plural. Elisions 'eg(o) aut', 'puls(um) arguet', 'sanguin(e) et', 'dom(um) atque', 'atqu(e) exutos'.

sentences.t:
Haud ita me experti Bitias et Pandarus ingens
et quos mille die victor sub Tartara misi,
inclusus muris hostilique aggere saeptus.
sentences.l:
Not so me tested Bitias and Pandarus huge
and those whom a thousand in a day, victor, under Tartarus I sent,
shut in by walls and by the hostile rampart hemmed.
sentences.i: That is not how I seemed to Bitias and huge Pandarus, or to the thousand I sent down to Tartarus in a single day of victory, though I was shut inside the walls and hemmed in by the enemy's rampart.
sentences.n: 'Haud ita me experti (sunt)', 'not so did they find me'. In Book IX Turnus burst into the Trojan camp when the giant brothers Pandarus and Bitias threw the gate open; he killed Bitias, then Pandarus, and many more before he escaped into the Tiber (IX.672–818). 'mille', a round figure for 'countless'. 'die', 'in one day', ablative of time. 'inclusus… saeptus', 'shut in… hemmed', the danger he fought through. Elisions 'm(e) experti', 'hostiliqu(e) aggere'.

sentences.t: “Nulla salus bello.
sentences.l: ‘No safety in war.’
sentences.i: ‘There is no safety in war,’ you say.
sentences.n: Drances' words of 362, thrown back at him by Turnus. The print sets an opening double mark before 'Nulla' and closes nothing here; l and i give just these three words in single marks, a quotation inside the speech, as at XI.252–293. 'Nulla salus bello', 'no safety in war', said with scorn. Turnus answers the slogan in the next unit. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Capiti cane talia, demens,
Dardanio rebusque tuis.
sentences.l:
To the head sing such things, madman,
the Dardanian, and to your own affairs.
sentences.i: Chant such things, madman, against the head of the Dardanian and for your own fortunes.
sentences.n: 'Capiti… Dardanio', 'to the Dardanian head', Aeneas's, split across the line-break. 'cane', 'sing, prophesy', 'cano' used of oracles and spells: prophesy such doom for Aeneas, not for us. 'rebusque tuis', 'and to your own affairs', your own party, since Drances is suspected of favouring the Trojans. 'demens', 'madman', the insults grow. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Proinde omnia magno
ne cessa turbare metu atque extollere vires
gentis bis victae, contra premere arma Latini.
sentences.l:
So all things with great
do not cease to throw into confusion with fear and to extol the strength
of a race twice conquered, on the other hand to press down the arms of Latinus.
sentences.i: So go on, never stop throwing everything into turmoil with your terrors, praising up the strength of a people twice beaten, and running down the arms of Latinus.
sentences.n: 'ne cessa', 'do not stop', the poetic negative imperative with 'ne', instead of prose 'noli'. 'omnia magno… metu', 'all things with great fear', framing. 'extollere vires gentis bis victae', 'to exalt the strength of a twice-conquered people': Troy fell twice, to Hercules in Laomedon's time and to the Greeks (Numanus's 'bis capti Phryges', IX.599). 'contra premere', 'by contrast to belittle', 'arma Latini', the king's side. Elisions 'Proind(e) omnia', 'met(u) atque', 'atqu(e) extollere', 'premer(e) arma'.

sentences.t:
Nunc et Myrmidonum proceres Phrygia arma tremescunt,
nunc et Tydides et Larissaeus Achilles,
amnis et Hadriacas retro fugit Aufidus undas.
sentences.l:
Now even the Myrmidons' chiefs at Phrygian arms tremble,
now even the son of Tydeus and Larissaean Achilles,
and the river from the Adriatic backwards flees, Aufidus, the waves.
sentences.i: Now, no doubt, the chiefs of the Myrmidons quake at Trojan arms, now Tydeus's son and Achilles of Larissa quake too, and the river Aufidus runs backward in flight from the Adriatic waves.
sentences.n: Sarcasm: if Drances is right, the world is upside down. 'Nunc et', 'now even'. The Myrmidons were Achilles' men; 'Phrygia arma', the Trojans'. 'Tydides', 'son of Tydeus', Diomedes, who has just refused to fight Aeneas (225–295). 'Larissaeus', from Larissa in Thessaly, Achilles' country; the pair echoes II.197, 'Tydides… Larisaeus Achilles'. 'amnis… Aufidus', a river of Apulia, Diomedes' new home, flowing into the Adriatic; a river running back to its source is a proverbial impossibility. Elision 'Phrygi(a) arma'.

sentences.t:
Vel cum se pavidum contra mea iurgia fingit
artificis scelus et formidine crimen acerbat.
sentences.l:
Or when himself afraid against my abuse he pretends,
the crime of a schemer, and with fear the charge makes bitter.
sentences.i: Or take the times when the scheming villain pretends to be frightened of my railing, and by his fear makes the accusation sharper.
sentences.n: A loose, angry construction: 'Vel cum', 'or (look) when', a fresh example of Drances' tricks, with no main clause. 'se pavidum… fingit', 'pretends himself afraid', as Drances did at 348 ('licet arma mihi mortemque minetur'). 'contra mea iurgia', 'in the face of my abuse'. 'artificis scelus', 'the villain of a trickster', 'scelus' 'crime' used of a person, an abusive idiom of comedy. 'formidine crimen acerbat', 'he sharpens the charge with his fear': pretending to fear Turnus makes Turnus look a tyrant. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Numquam animam talem dextra hac, absiste moveri,
amittes: habitet tecum et sit pectore in isto.
sentences.l:
Never a soul such by this right hand, cease to be troubled,
will you lose: let it dwell with you and be in that breast.
sentences.i: Never will you lose such a soul as yours by this right hand of mine (put away your alarm): let it live on with you and stay in that breast of yours.
sentences.n: 'animam talem', 'such a soul', with contempt: a soul not worth the taking. 'dextra hac', 'by this right hand', ablative of means. 'absiste moveri', 'cease to be disturbed', a mocking parenthesis. 'amittes', 'you will lose', the future, held to the next line. 'habitet… sit', jussive subjunctives: let it stay where it belongs. 'pectore in isto', 'in that breast of yours', 'iste' again contemptuous. Elisions 'Numqu(am) animam', 'dextr(a) hac', 'tec(um) et', 'pector(e) in'.

sentences.t: Nunc ad te et tua magna, pater, consulta revertor.
sentences.l: Now to you and your great, father, proposals I return.
sentences.i: Now, father, I come back to you and to your weighty proposals.
sentences.n: Turnus turns from Drances to Latinus. 'pater', 'father', a respectful address to the king, who is also the father of his promised bride. 'tua magna… consulta', 'your great proposals', the land and ships offered to the Trojans (316–334), the adjective and noun around the vocative. 'revertor', deponent, 'I return'. Elision 't(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Si nullam nostris ultra spem ponis in armis,
si tam deserti sumus et semel agmine verso
funditus occidimus neque habet Fortuna regressum?
oremus pacem et dextras tendamus inertis.
sentences.l:
If no further hope in our you place arms,
if so deserted we are and, once the column turned,
utterly we have fallen and Fortune has no return? —
let us beg for peace and hands let us stretch out helpless.
sentences.i: If you place no further hope in our arms, if we are so forsaken and utterly lost because our line broke once, and Fortune has no way back? — then let us pray for peace and hold out our hands, defenceless.
sentences.n: The print sets a question mark after 'regressum' and goes on with a small 'oremus', Greenough's habit after a question (as at I.583 and VI.845): the 'si'-clauses rise to an indignant question before the answer. It is kept as printed, and the reading text marks the turn with a dash. 'ultra', 'any longer'. 'semel agmine verso', ablative absolute, 'the line once turned', one defeat. 'neque habet Fortuna regressum', 'and Fortune has no way back'. 'oremus… tendamus', hortatory subjunctives. 'dextras… inertis', 'hands without weapons', the suppliant's gesture. Elisions 'nequ(e) habet', 'pac(em) et'.

sentences.t: Quamquam O, si solitae quicquam virtutis adesset!
sentences.l: And yet, O, if anything of our usual valour were present!
sentences.i: And yet, oh, if only there were anything left of our old courage!
sentences.n: 'Quamquam', 'and yet', correcting what has just been said: Turnus cannot bring himself to accept surrender. 'O si… adesset', a wish for the present that cannot be fulfilled, the imperfect subjunctive. 'quicquam… virtutis', 'anything of valour', the partitive genitive. 'solitae', 'accustomed', the courage the Latins used to have. Elision 'Quamqu(am) O'.

sentences.t:
Ille mihi ante alios fortunatusque laborum
egregiusque animi, qui, nequid tale videret,
procubuit moriens et humum semel ore momordit.
sentences.l:
That man to me before others both fortunate in his toils
and outstanding in spirit, who, so that not anything such he should see,
fell dying and the ground once with his mouth bit.
sentences.i: In my eyes that man is blessed in his labours beyond all others, and noblest in spirit, who fell dying, once and for all biting the earth, rather than see such a thing.
sentences.n: 'mihi', 'to me', 'in my judgement', the ethic dative. 'fortunatus laborum', 'fortunate in his toils', a genitive of respect after the Greek model; 'egregius animi', 'outstanding in spirit', 'animi' an old locative-genitive. 'nequid tale videret', a purpose clause, 'so as not to see any such thing', printed as one word ('ne quid'). 'humum… ore momordit', 'bit the ground with his mouth', the Homeric picture of a warrior falling face down (Iliad II.418, from memory). Elisions 'mih(i) ante', 'ant(e) alios', 'egregiusqu(e) animi'.

sentences.t:
Sin et opes nobis et adhuc intacta iuventus
auxilioque urbes Italae populique supersunt,
sin et Troianis cum multo gloria venit
sanguine, sunt illis sua funera parque per omnis
tempestas:
sentences.l:
But if both resources to us and still untouched youth
and for help Italian cities and peoples remain,
but if even to the Trojans, with much, glory has come,
blood, there are for them their own deaths, and equal over all
the storm:
sentences.i: But if we still have resources and young men untouched by war, and cities and peoples of Italy remain to help us, and if the Trojans too have won their glory at the cost of much blood (they have their own dead, and the same storm has passed over all):
sentences.n: 'Sin', 'but if', the other side of 411: two 'sin' clauses balance the earlier 'si' clauses. 'opes nobis… supersunt', 'resources remain to us', dative of possession. 'auxilio', 'for help', dative of purpose. 'cum multo… sanguine', 'with much blood', framing 'gloria venit'. 'sunt illis sua funera', 'they have their own deaths', 'illis', dative of possession. 'parque per omnis tempestas', 'and the storm (went) equally through all', the verb left out; 'omnis', '-is' accusative plural. Elision 'auxilioqu(e) urbes'.

sentences.t:
cur indecores in limine primo
deficimus?
sentences.l:
why, inglorious, on the threshold first
do we fail?
sentences.i: why do we lose heart so shamefully on the very threshold?
sentences.n: The question answers the long 'sin' clauses. 'indecores', 'without honour', an adjective used for the manner, 'shamefully'. 'in limine primo', 'at the first threshold', at the beginning of the struggle, as if they were turning back at the door. 'deficimus', 'we fail, lose heart', held over to the next line for weight. No elisions.

sentences.t: Cur ante tubam tremor occupat artus?
sentences.l: Why before the trumpet trembling seizes our limbs?
sentences.i: Why does trembling seize our limbs before the trumpet has even sounded?
sentences.n: A second 'cur', in parallel, an anaphora. 'ante tubam', 'before the trumpet', before the signal for battle has been given. 'tremor occupat artus', 'trembling takes hold of our limbs', the physical sign of fear, a phrase of epic. Turnus turns the charge of cowardice back on the whole council. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Multa dies variisque labor mutabilis aevi
rettulit in melius, multos alterna revisens
lusit et in solido rursus Fortuna locavit.
sentences.l:
Many things the day and with varied (turns) the toil of changeable time
has brought back to better, many, alternately revisiting,
has mocked and on the solid again Fortune has set.
sentences.i: Many a time the passing days and the shifting toil of changing time have turned things for the better; Fortune comes back by turns to many she has mocked and sets them again on firm ground.
sentences.n: 'variisque', as printed, is hard to construe; the Latin Library reads 'variique', 'and the toil of varied, changeable time', and some texts are said to read 'variusque', 'and varied toil'. The print is kept, read as 'with its varied turns'; the sense is the same either way. 'Multa', neuter plural object, 'many things'. 'dies', 'time, the passing of days', the subject. 'rettulit in melius', 'brought back to better'. 'alterna revisens', 'revisiting by turns'. 'lusit', 'made sport of'. 'in solido', 'on solid ground', the opposite of Fortune's wheel. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Non erit auxilio nobis Aetolus et Arpi:
at Messapus erit felixque Tolumnius et quos
tot populi misere duces, nec parva sequetur
gloria delectos Latio et Laurentibus agris.
sentences.l:
Not will be for help to us the Aetolian and Arpi:
but Messapus will, and fortunate Tolumnius, and those whom
so many peoples have sent, leaders, nor small will follow
glory the chosen from Latium and the Laurentine fields.
sentences.i: The Aetolian and his Arpi will be no help to us: but Messapus will, and lucky Tolumnius, and the leaders sent by so many peoples, and no small glory will attend the chosen men of Latium and the fields of Laurentum.
sentences.n: 'erit auxilio nobis', 'will be for a help to us', the double dative, singular with two subjects. 'Aetolus', Diomedes, called Aetolian after his father's country (as at 239); 'Arpi', the city he founded in Apulia. Messapus led a contingent in VII.691–705; Tolumnius is the augur who will break the truce at XII.258. 'misere' = 'miserunt', the perfect in '-ere'. 'delectos', 'the chosen men', the picked forces. 'Laurentibus agris', of Laurentum, Latinus's city. Elision 'Lati(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Est et Volscorum egregia de gente Camilla,
agmen agens equitum et florentis aere catervas.
sentences.l:
There is also from the Volscians' outstanding race Camilla,
a column driving of horsemen and flowering with bronze troops.
sentences.i: We have Camilla too, of the noble race of the Volscians, leading a column of horse and squadrons gleaming with bronze.
sentences.n: 'Est et', 'there is also', the name kept to the end of the line. Camilla, the warrior maiden of the Volsci, closed the catalogue of Italian forces in VII.803–817 and will have her great scenes later in this book. 'agmen agens', 'driving a column', the noun and verb from the same root. 'florentis aere catervas', 'troops flowering with bronze', bright armour pictured as blossom; 'florentis', '-is' accusative plural. The second line repeats VII.804 word for word. Elisions 'Volscor(um) egregia', 'equit(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Quod si me solum Teucri in certamina poscunt
idque placet tantumque bonis communibus obsto,
non adeo has exosa manus Victoria fugit,
ut tanta quicquam pro spe temptare recusem.
sentences.l:
But if me alone the Teucrians into combat call,
and this pleases, and so much the common good I stand in the way of,
not so much these, hating them, hands Victory has fled,
that for so great anything a hope to attempt I should refuse.
sentences.i: But if the Trojans challenge me alone to combat, and you are content with that, and I am so great an obstacle to the common good, Victory has not so hated and fled these hands of mine that I would refuse any venture for so great a prize.
sentences.n: Turnus answers Drances' challenge (373–375). 'me solum… poscunt', 'demand me alone'. 'idque placet', 'and that is agreed', by the council. 'tantum… obsto', 'I stand so much in the way', with the dative 'bonis communibus'. 'exosa', 'hating', the participle of the defective verb 'exodi', active in sense. 'non adeo… ut… recusem', a result clause, 'not so far… that I should refuse'. 'pro spe', 'for (so great) a hope'. Victoria is a goddess here, as at Rome. Elisions 'Teucr(i) in', 'ade(o) has'.

sentences.t:
Ibo animis contra, vel magnum praestet Achillem
factaque Vulcani manibus paria induat arma
ille licet.
sentences.l:
I will go with spirit against him, even if great he should play Achilles
and made by Vulcan's hands equal should put on arms,
he, though he may.
sentences.i: I will go against him boldly, even if he should prove a great Achilles and put on armour like his, made by the hands of Vulcan.
sentences.n: 'Ibo animis contra', 'I will go against (him) with courage', 'animis' plural for spirit. 'vel… licet', 'even though', 'licet' with the subjunctive, held to the end of the sentence. 'praestet', 'show himself as, equal'. Achilles' armour was made by Hephaestus (Iliad XVIII, from memory); Aeneas's by Vulcan at Venus's request (VIII.608–731), which Turnus has not yet faced. 'paria', 'matching (Achilles')'. 'ille', Aeneas, unnamed, held back for emphasis. Elisions 'Ib(o) animis', 'pari(a) induat'.

sentences.t:
Vobis animam hanc soceroque Latino
Turnus ego, haud ulli veterum virtute secundus,
“devovi.
sentences.l:
To you this life and to my father-in-law Latinus
I, Turnus, not to any of the men of old in valour second,
have devoted.
sentences.i: To you and to Latinus, my father-in-law, I, Turnus, second to none of the heroes of old in valour, have vowed this life of mine.
sentences.n: The print has '“devovi', a misprint for 'devovi', corrected here: the opening mark is stray, since Turnus's speech runs on and no new one begins. 'Vobis… soceroque Latino', datives, 'to you and to my father-in-law'; 'socer' anticipates the marriage. 'Turnus ego', the proud name. 'devovi', 'I have devoted', the Roman 'devotio', in which a general vowed his life to the gods below in exchange for victory, as the Decii did. Elisions 'anim(am) hanc', 'eg(o) haud'.

sentences.t:
Solum Aeneas vocat: et vocet oro,
nec Drances potius, sive est haec ira deorum,
morte luat, sive est virtus et gloria, tollat.”
sentences.l:
Me alone Aeneas calls: and let him call, I pray,
and not Drances rather, whether this is the anger of the gods,
with death atone, or whether it is valour and glory, carry it off.”
sentences.i: Aeneas calls on me alone: then let him call, I pray, and let it not be Drances rather than I who, if this is the anger of the gods, pays for it with his death, or, if it is valour and glory, carries off the prize.”
sentences.n: 'Solum', 'me alone', the object of 'vocat'. 'et vocet oro', 'and let him call, I pray', 'oro' standing alone with the subjunctive. 'nec Drances potius… luat… tollat', 'and let Drances not rather (than I)… atone or… take (the glory)'. The two 'sive' clauses cover both outcomes: if the gods are angry, Turnus will pay with his life; if there is glory to win, it will be his. 'morte luat', 'atone with death'. Elisions 'Solu(m) Aeneas', 'siv(e) est' twice.
